title: Interest: simple and compound
blurb: How money grows when it earns interest, and why time matters so much.
t1.title: What interest is
t1.hook: Sana puts {P} in a savings plan that pays {r} a year. Your mission: understand how that money grows.
t1.define: **Interest** is the price of using money. The money you start with is the **principal**. The **rate** is the interest per year, as a percentage.
t1.example: In one year, {P} at {r} earns {yr1}. That is {P} × {r}.
q1.opt.a: The price paid for using someone else's money
q1.opt.b: A fee for opening a bank account
q1.opt.c: The part of a company that you own
q1.hint: Think about who pays whom, and what for.
q1.explain: Interest is the price paid for using someone else's money.
q2.prompt: Ravi lends {sP} at {sr} a year. How much interest does he earn in one year? Type a number in rupees.
q2.hint: Multiply the amount by the rate.
t2.title: Simple interest
t2.define: **Simple interest** is paid only on the money you started with. So the interest is the same every year.
t2.steps.2: Years 2 and 3: the same {yr1} each year, because the base never changes
t2.steps.3: After {y3} years: {yr3} of interest, so {tot3} in total
t2.formula: Simple interest = principal × rate × years. Write the rate as a decimal. Example: ₹2,000 at 5% for 4 years is 2,000 × 0.05 × 4 = ₹400.
q3.prompt: Ravi lends {sP} at {sr} simple interest for {sy} years. How much interest does he earn in total? Type a number in rupees.
q3.hint: Work out one year of interest, then multiply by the number of years.
q4.prompt: With simple interest, how does the interest earned in year 3 compare with year 1?
q4.opt.b: It is bigger, because the money has grown
q4.hint: Look at the steps above. What is the interest worked out on each year?
q4.explain: Simple interest is always worked out on the starting amount, so every year gives the same interest.
t3.title: Compound interest
t3.define: **Compound interest** is paid on your money and on the interest you already earned. So the interest grows each year.
t3.analogy: Picture two mango trees. One gives only its own fruit. The other drops seeds, and each seed grows a new tree. Compound interest is the second tree.
t3.steps.4: Simple gave {tot3}. Compound gave {c3}. The extra {extra3} is interest on interest.
t3.formula: Compound amount = principal × (1 + rate)^years. The small raised number means multiply (1 + rate) by itself that many times. Example: ₹2,000 at 5% for 2 years is 2,000 × 1.05 × 1.05 = ₹2,205.
t3.explore: Open the lab. The grey line is simple interest and the green line is compound. Move the sliders, then answer the questions.
q5.prompt: {lp} grows at {lr} a year, with interest added once a year. How much will it be after {ly} years? Type a number in rupees.
q5.hint: Grow it for one year, then grow the new total for another year.
q5.explain: {lp} becomes {cq5a} after year 1, then {cq5} after year 2.
q6.prompt: In the lab, set the rate to {labRate} and the years to {labYears}. What does {P} become with compound interest? Type a number in rupees.
q6.hint: Read the compound amount under the chart. You can type it with or without commas.
q6.explain: At {labRate} for {labYears} years, {P} compounds to {labAnswer}. Simple interest would give only {labSimple}.
q7.prompt: Which grows faster over many years?
q7.opt.a: Compound interest, because it earns interest on interest
q7.opt.b: Simple interest, because it is easier to work out
q7.opt.c: They always give the same amount
q7.fb.c: They only match in the first year. After that, compound interest also earns on past interest, so it pulls ahead.
q7.hint: Look at the grey and green lines in the lab.
q7.explain: Compound interest also earns on past interest, so it pulls further ahead every year.
t4.title: Rule of 72
t4.define: The **Rule of 72** is a quick way to estimate how long money takes to double. Divide 72 by the yearly rate.
t4.steps.1: At {r4} a year, the rate is {r4n}
t4.steps.3: So money doubles in about {d4} years at {r4}
q8.prompt: Money grows at {rate9} a year. About how many years does it take to double? Type a number.
q8.hint: Divide 72 by the rate, written as a plain number.
q9.prompt: A saver's money doubles in about {d6} years. About what yearly rate is that? Type a percentage.
q9.hint: Turn the rule around: divide 72 by the number of years.
q9.explain: 72 ÷ {d6} is {ans9}, so the rate is about {ans9} percent a year.
t5.title: Start early
t5.story: Asha starts saving {m} a month at age {a1}. Ravi starts at age {a2}. Both stop at {stop}, and their money grows at {sipRate} a year.
t5.define: Time is the strongest lever. Money saved early has more years to earn interest on interest.
t5.explore: Open the lab. Change the starting age and watch the final amount.
t5.mistake: Some people think starting ten years later is almost the same. Try it in the lab before you decide.
q10.prompt: In the lab, set the age to {a1}. How much does the saver have at the end? Type a number in rupees.
q10.hint: Read the green number labelled value at the end.
q10.explain: Saving {m} a month from age {a1} to {stop} grows to {early}.
q11.prompt: Now set the age to {a2}. How much does the saver have at the end?
q11.explain: Starting at {a2} grows to {late}. That is far less, after losing only {gap} years.
q12.prompt: Ravi starts {gap} years later than Asha. Compared with Asha, his final amount is…
q12.fb.a: Ten extra years is a long time. Interest on interest builds slowly at first and then fast, and the late starter misses that part.
q12.fb.b: It feels like a small gap, but it is not. The early years of growth are the ones that compound the most.
q12.hint: Compare the two final amounts you just read from the lab.
q12.explain: {late} is less than half of {early}. Starting early matters more than most people expect.
glossary.interest.def: The price paid for using someone else's money.
glossary.principal.def: The original amount of money you save or borrow.
glossary.simple_interest.def: Interest paid only on the original amount.
glossary.compound_interest.def: Interest paid on the original amount and on earlier interest.
glossary.rate.def: The interest charged or earned, as a percentage per year.
glossary.rule_of_72.def: Divide 72 by the rate to estimate years to double.
